verdicts.note: 'the vast number of things' keeps Jowett's hyperbole ('the world of things') without the Victorian idiom that can be heard as the physical world. The sense matches Plato's 'many and varied things', and it reads naturally.
A pure reorder. 'that' now comes right after 'attribute', so it is heard as the object (Agathon's supposed lack of refinement), not as the start of a clause. Nothing is added or lost.
'that is' marks the apposition, so the listener hears one people, not two. This is the same device as 7.60 'Lacedaemon, that is, Sparta', and it adds no content.

The gloss is accurate: the word behind Jowett's 'beautiful' also means fine and noble, and 'fine and noble' echoes Jowett's own pairing 'fair and noble' at 7.60 and 7.63. It is given once, at the premise the argument turns on, so 'the good is also beautiful' no longer sounds arbitrary, and the logic of 7.42 is unchanged. It is heard as Socrates' own elaboration inside the question, not as an editor's note. 'isn't' is Socrates' normal register.

An accurate unpacking of the core metaphor, grounded in Jowett's own text: 7.54 (beauty presides at birth; 'when approaching beauty' the conceiving power bears fruit; beauty 'whose approach' relieves labor) and 7.60 ('the touch of the beautiful which is ever present to his memory'). It keeps the glossary's 'giving birth' and the pregnancy image. It does not pre-empt Diotima's explanation that everyone is pregnant, so Socrates' 'I do not understand you' still makes sense. 'whether of body or of soul' still follows 'beauty', as in round 2. Diotima uses no contraction here.

The problem is real. To a listener, 'the knowledge of beauty everywhere' flatly contradicts the next paragraph, where this beauty exists in no other being and in no place. Removing 'everywhere' is the right resolution, and it takes nothing from another translation. It also needs no Greek: Jowett's own 'To this I will proceed' already renders Plato's forward reference ('beauty of this kind', meaning the kind about to be described), so dropping the contradictory word and folding that announcement in resolves it entirely within Jowett's words. The chosen wording has four problems. It adds 'very special', an intensifier in neither Jowett nor Plato. It repeats 'kind' ('a single kind of knowledge ... of a very special kind') and 'very' ('very special ... very best attention'). It uses the count noun 'a beauty', which by ear can mean a beautiful person. And 'I will now go on to that beauty' can be heard as Diotima herself going on to the beauty rather than to the topic. The replacement keeps 'single', the forward reference and the suspense, and ends at the semicolon, so ' please give me your very best attention:' follows unchanged.
verdicts.proposed_replace: he is at last granted the vision of a single kind of knowledge, the knowledge of the beauty I will now describe;

verdicts.note: Jowett's 'true love' now reads as the romantic cliche, the opposite of his sense (love of the right kind). The replacement keeps both parts: 'true' -> 'in the right way' and 'love' -> 'loving'. It takes the object from Jowett's own context: the ascent begins by loving one youth (7.62-7.63), and 7.65 names 'beautiful boys and young men'. The frankness matches Plato's word ('loving boys rightly') without sharpening it. 'Loving' adds nothing sexual, and 'young man' follows the successor's rendering of Jowett's 'youth' and the glossary's definition of the beloved. It also stays consistent with Pausanias's line against loving young boys (3.2). The wording is not another translation's. 'From these' still refers back to the other beautiful things, and the sentence reads cleanly.

Plato uses the same word at 7.63 and 7.65; Jowett renders it 'institutions' at 7.63 and 'practices' at 7.65. Using Jowett's own 7.63 word in both places lets the listener match the recap to the first ladder. It is a choice between Jowett's words, not an import.
Jowett's 'garments', listed alongside gold, means finery. 'fine clothes' restores the sense of luxury and removes the bathos. Here 'fine' means costly, which does not clash with the 7.40 gloss.
Jowett's 'vanities' means empty, worthless things, but a modern listener hears it as conceit. 'empty trifles' gives Jowett's meaning.
Restores Jowett's exact phrase and Eryximachus's pompous officialese, which echoes 'proposal' (1.43) and 'motion' (1.47). It is clear by ear and not archaic.
Restores Jowett's 'confessed', which echoes 8.24 'he makes me confess'.
Matches Jowett and 8.31 'at my wit's end' in the same speech. The two spellings sound the same, so this is consistency only.

Follows the glossary rule 'fair' (of persons) -> 'beautiful'. It matches 8.3 'the most beautiful person here', which refers to the same man, and carries the beauty theme into Alcibiades' speech. Jowett's order (fairest, then wisest) is kept.

Alcibiades' sentence runs on into 8.12, which reopens with a single quote. Leaving the single quote open follows the convention and matches 8.33-8.35. The nested double quotes around the verse are intact.
Restores Jowett's emphatic 'myself' ('I was myself one of those'), which answers Pausanias's 'most of you are in the same state' in 1.36. It reads naturally.

Removing 'his lover' ends both the redundancy and the misparse. By ear, 'granting physical favors — to a bad lover' now runs on correctly across the dash. The gloss stays frank and accurate, and stays attached to 'yielding'.

Jowett's 'us' is a generic 'one'. Once the paragraph defines yielding as the beloved's act, 'the beloved' is the only coherent reading, so the edit chooses between readings Jowett's words allow and imports nothing. It fits the next sentence ('encourages lovers to pursue and the beloved to flee') and 3.7-3.8.
'justly' is Jowett's own word ('can justly be censured'), and it removes 'fair' used to mean just, as the glossary requires.

In Jowett's line, 'First in the train of gods' could describe either the maker or Love. Phaedrus cites the line to prove that Love is the eldest god. Placing the phrase after 'Love' takes the only reading that serves that argument, and it matches the Greek grammar. It also avoids the everyday phrase 'first of all' and gives a clean pentameter. 'He' (Generation, from 2.2) is kept, as in Jowett.
'comes back' already means 'again', so Jowett's 'has to be repeated' is fully rendered. The later 'And again it tells of Polyhymnia' is a separate 'again' and correctly remains.

Fixes a real listener problem. In modern English 'blamed' implies moral fault, which clashes with 'not thought to be doing anything dishonorable' and with the encouragement just described. 'thought disgraced' takes Jowett's 'blamed' in its older sense of 'censured' and fits Pausanias's honor/shame vocabulary: it ties to 'dishonorable' earlier in the same sentence and to 'disgraceful' in 3.5. 'wins his beloved' only unpacks 'succeeds'. The contest image makes it clear that the disgrace attaches to failing, not to the pursuit, so the sentence no longer seems to contradict itself. 'admired' for Jowett's 'praised' was not needed, since 'praised' is plain English. But it is a harmless near-synonym that pairs with 'thought disgraced', and it adds no claim. The frankness is not sharpened.
'plead' keeps the humble begging of 'supplicate' in an everyday word. The list keeps four verbs, like Jowett's pray, entreat, supplicate, swear.

Restores Jowett's 'something', which matches 7.0 (father) and 7.8 (Love), where Plato uses the same word. The slight oddity of 'the brother of something' is the point of the analogy, and 7.6 answers it at once ('of a brother or sister').

Renders Jowett's 'the remark was a just one' and avoids 'fair' used to mean just, one sentence before 'Love is the love of beauty'. Socrates' irony survives: he praises a remark he is about to use against Agathon.
Jowett's 'a man' is a generic 'one'. Using the same word as 7.32 helps the listener recognize the premise when it is recalled. This modernizes Jowett's generic; it imports nothing.
The recalled premise now repeats 7.52's formula exactly ('the love of the everlasting possession of the good') and matches the conclusion 'the love of immortality'. There is no contraction.
Uses the same formula as 7.54 and is clearer by ear than the elliptical 'love is of the immortal'. Jowett's content is unchanged.

Jowett's own capitalization is inconsistent: 'Love' at 7.34, 'love' at 7.38 and 7.42. Throughout 7.34-7.42 the subject is the god, and the successor already has 'Love' at 7.34 and 7.38, so 'Love' is right here.

paragraph_problems.issue: Side effect of R3-7 (minor, not blocking). In round 2, 7.64 'beauty absolute ... simple' echoed 7.65 'absolute beauty' (twice) and 'that true beauty, simple and divine': Jowett uses the same words, and Plato uses the same terms. After R3-7, 7.64 says 'beauty itself ... one in form', while 7.65 still says 'absolute beauty' and 'simple'. The recap can still be followed. But a first-time listener now meets 'absolute beauty' as a new term, and may hear 'simple' as 'plain'. There are two optional fixes. One restores Jowett's word at the climax: 'It is absolute beauty — beauty itself, existing by itself and in itself, always one in form, and everlasting.' The other changes 7.65's 'simple and divine' to 'one in form and divine'.

Pre-existing, not caused by any R3 edit, and optional. 'a man could fairly argue' uses 'fair' to mean just or reasonable, the same class that R3-20 (3.2) and R3-26 (7.30) removed under the glossary rule. A consistent fix would be 'a man could reasonably argue'. Outside this packet, 8.14 'it is hardly fair to compare' is the same class.

summary: 30 R3 edits across 25 paragraphs: 29 accept, 1 revise (R3-6), 0 reject. The final text matches the packet's AFTER texts exactly, and every word-level change from round 2 corresponds to a listed edit. The conventions hold in all 25 paragraphs: straight quotes, reopened quotes, American spelling, spaced em dashes, no ellipses or double spaces, and no contractions from Diotima. Flagged items: 7.63 (R3-6) resolves a real contradiction and is not an import, but it can be done within Jowett's words, since his 'To this I will proceed' already carries Plato's forward reference. 'a beauty of a very special kind' adds an intensifier and reads awkwardly, so the verdict is revise, with a replacement. 7.64 (R3-7) loses nothing of Jowett's, and each term is mapped. (R3-8): 'loving a young man in the right way' keeps both parts of 'true love' and matches Plato's frankness without sharpening it. The glosses at 7.40 ('fine and noble', which echoes Jowett's 'fair and noble') and 7.53 ('giving birth in the presence of beauty', grounded in Jowett's 7.54 and 7.60) are accurate. At 3.4, 'thought disgraced' is a sound modern reading of 'blamed'; 'admired' for 'praised' was optional but harmless. At 3.6, 'the beloved' is the only coherent reading of Jowett's generic 'us'. At 2.3, the reorder takes the reading Phaedrus's argument needs. Every edit that cites Plato either chooses between readings Jowett's words allow or corrects a real contradiction, and none takes another translation's wording. Minor follow-ups: the lost 7.64/7.65 echo of 'absolute' and 'simple', and a leftover 'fairly' meaning 'reasonably' at 3.5 (and 'fair' at 8.14).
